My best moment was the “Hah!” that spontaneously flew out when I saw the “fair game” meaning for BALLOON POP.  

And there were more sweet puzzle offshoots.  With [Greek salad morsel], as I was cataloguing the possibilities, when I landed on OLIVE, I actually tasted one even though I wasn’t eating one, tasted that one-of-a-kind marvelous flavor.

With HERMITS, my brain shot back to that forever-ago group, Herman’s Hermits, and I remembered their catchy song, one II haven’t thought about in decades, “I’m Henry VIII, I Am”.  I believe that song will be with me all day.

But listen to this from crossnerd me.  Dana, the constructor, has a chance to make crossword history.  This is his third Times puzzle, and they’ve come in order – Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday.  Only one constructor (Andrew Ries) has hit the cycle (a puzzle for every day of the week) in their first seven puzzles, but no one has done it IN ORDER.

Go for it, Dana, and thank you for those sweet moments today!

I figured that the blog would tell me and if it didn't, I could always Google it.  But I really wanted to try and guess what a game called BALLOON POP, "requiring precision", might look like.  I quickly rejected my first thought: balloons spinning like crazy past a stationary carnival-goer holding a pin.  I rejected that in favor of this: It's the carnival-goer with the pin that's being spun dizzyingly in some sort of spinning machine past a bunch of unmoving balloons.  Can you see it in your mind's eye?  All the vertiginous "thrills" of the Roller Coaster and the Cyclone to be found in a pop-the-balloon game.

What BALLOON POP really is turns out to be rather prosaic by comparison.

I'll grant you the theme was OK, but how was this Monday/Tuesday difficulty *grid* "clever"? You point out the disappointing clues yourself. Do you distinguish between the grid and clues being clever in some way I simply can't grasp?

@Andrzej

Sorry: I meant “clever” to apply to theme and “excellent” to both the theme and grid, I should have been clearer. I wouldn’t call the grid clever but it is pretty excellent in the sense that the fill is solid with not a lot of glue, which is about the most you can expect from an early week puzzle and actually much more difficult to accomplish than you might realize. 

That said, it’s possible to spice up almost any common term with a fresher clue and this puzzle didn’t even want to attempt that—at least they could have with the themers. And the theme, while clever, was not really a Wednesday level (I define that as a theme where the themers are common phrases without a lot of wordplay). I was surprised that jt wasn’t a Monday or Tuesday.

So call my comment a Lewis-ianish attempt to accentuate the positives and not overstate my overall disappointment. I think we were on the same page in our assessment.

@SP

Let Lewis be Lewis and look to me more often, please 😃

@Andrzej

And if it wasn’t clear, I do distinguish between the grid and the clues. You can have a terrific grid with poor or uninteresting clues; and you can have a poor grid with a lot of glue, obscure terms, or in your case trivia, but a lot of clever clues for the rest. The clueing is mostly the responsibility of editors, so it’s not an insult to the constructor to call that out.

@Andrzej

So for example, if you have a grid with a lot of abbreviations, Roman numerals, obscure names or trivia (that couldn’t be clued better), partial phrases (ASEAT: Take ___) etc. that would be suboptimal. 

This one? Not much stands out to me as bad. Some complain about RONA but I’ve heard it before and it could have been clued more naturally. CCED and ATAD are pretty standard. ENBY I hadn’t heard but sounds like it’s reasonably common usage now so I can’t complain about that. So I think this is a very good grid. A bit boring maybe and probably more Mondayish but very well done. And if they really wanted to make this a Wednesday then they could have at least made some of the clues cleverer (or even a bit ambiguous to make it more challenging). 

That’s kind of a minimum for a good grid early week. Of course that won’t fly for the weekend themeless, then they are looking for fresher and more sparkling entries in the grid (and a lower word count).

Does that help clarify? And also, yes it really does sμcκ for a constructor when you think you have a perfect fun clue and the editors change it. They are often right but not always as we have seen when constructors show us their favorite changed clues in their notes. That’s one advantage and disadvantage of Crosshare puzzles—the clues are all mine, for better or worse.

@Big chungus

I'm sure I am, for the most part, preaching to the choir, but I can't help but want to try to get people to really focus on gender dysphoria.  I gave a flip response above, but it's a real, and life-altering condition.

If you don't have it, good for you.  But it is real.  Just like a lot of diseases that some people refuse to admit exists until they experience it, it is very real and it wreaks  havoc with people's lives.  For example, NYT columnist Ross Douthat belittled those suffering from Lyme disease, until he had it.

Try to think of it like this.  The sexual organs are the hardware, but the brain is the software.  As relatively simple as genitalia are, the brain is enormously complex, and prone to a multitude of maladies.  And just because you don't have any of them doesn't mean they don't exist.

At one time, and maybe still, a lot of people used  load a unix-like operating system, Linux, on their PCs.  So the computer looked like a PC but behaved like a unix machine.

This is just an analogy, but I hope it can lead some people to understand that the "jest pull down yer pants and look" people will  reconsider, and show at least a little compassion for these people.

@Francis
Speaking as what I understand is called a cis-woman, I'm not sure that saying that gender dysphoria is a disease or malady is going to help. I agree with the analogy and that it's a mis-fit between psychological perception and physical construction. But I believe that those who live with it would rather be seen as just another 'variety of normal'.
